topic.title: Why the rich borrow against their shares instead of selling

title: Why billionaires never sell their stock 🤫
description:
Selling is how most people get their money out. The very rich borrow instead. Here's why.
Illustrative only. Not financial advice.
cta: Did you know this one? Comment

lines.text: Billionaires almost never sell their stock. They borrow against it.
Wait, what? Why borrow if you're rich?
Sell a million dollars of stock he got for almost nothing, and tax can take $200,000.
Borrow a million against it? A loan isn't income. No tax at all.
And the stock he didn't sell keeps growing. At 8% a year, $2.2M in 10 years.
Sure. As long as the stock grows faster than the interest, the rich get richer. And when it falls, the bank can sell it for you.
So that's why billionaires almost never sell their stock.

US Short, no sourced facts. Loans are not taxable income (IRS: borrowed money is not income), so borrowing against shares triggers no tax; selling triggers capital gains tax, federal long-term rate up to 20% plus 3.8% net investment income tax, shown as '20%+'; the script assumes stock bought for almost nothing so the whole sale is gain. Margin risk stated: when the stock falls the lender can sell it. 8% a year growth is an assumption. No advice, no named stock; description carries the disclaimer.
